rule: To survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion under Rule 8(a)(2), a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face, meaning factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable. Courts apply a two-pronged approach. First, disregard legal conclusions and threadbare recitals of the elements, which get no assumption of truth. Second, assume the well-pleaded factual allegations are true and ask whether they plausibly give rise to an entitlement to relief. The Twombly standard governs all civil actions.
holding: No. The complaint's allegations of discriminatory purpose are conclusory and not entitled to the assumption of truth, and the remaining factual allegations do not plausibly show that petitioners adopted the detention policy for a discriminatory purpose. Reversed and remanded, with the Court of Appeals to decide in the first instance whether to remand to the District Court so Iqbal can seek leave to amend. (Kennedy, J., for the Court; Souter, Stevens, Ginsburg, and Breyer, JJ., dissenting.)

case_name: Bates v. State Bar of Arizona
rule: A state may not impose a blanket ban on lawyer advertising. Under the First Amendment, a state may not discipline a lawyer for a truthful newspaper advertisement of the availability and prices of routine legal services. It may still restrain false, deceptive, or misleading advertising, impose reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions, and suppress advertising of illegal transactions. A state supreme court's disciplinary rule restricting lawyer advertising is immune from Sherman Act attack under the Parker v. Brown state-action exemption, because the restraint is the State's own clearly articulated and actively supervised command.
holding: No as to the Sherman Act, because the rule is state action exempt under Parker v. Brown; yes as to the First Amendment, because truthful advertising of the availability and terms of routine legal services may not be subjected to blanket suppression; affirmed in part and reversed in part (opinion by Justice Blackmun).

rule: To survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, a complaint must plead "enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face." Labels, conclusions, and a formulaic recitation of the elements will not do, and factual allegations, taken as true, must raise a right to relief above the speculative level. For a Sherman Act § 1 claim, allegations of parallel conduct must be placed in a context that raises a suggestion of a preceding agreement; parallel conduct plus a bare assertion of conspiracy is insufficient.
holding: No. Under Rule 8(a)(2), a § 1 complaint must plead enough factual matter, taken as true, to plausibly suggest that an agreement was made. Because these allegations did not cross "the line from conceivable to plausible," the complaint "must be dismissed." The Second Circuit's judgment was reversed and the case remanded for further proceedings consistent with the opinion (Souter, J., for the Court; Stevens, J., dissenting, joined by Ginsburg, J., except as to Part IV).

rule: The prosecution violates due process when it suppresses evidence favorable to an accused, after the accused has requested it, if that evidence is material either to guilt or to punishment. The prosecution's good faith or bad faith is irrelevant. The remedy may be limited to a new trial on punishment where, under state law, the suppressed evidence could not have affected the verdict on guilt.
holding: No. Suppression of requested evidence favorable to the accused violates due process when the evidence is material to guilt or punishment, regardless of the prosecution's good or bad faith, but limiting the new trial to punishment did not violate due process or equal protection because under Maryland law the court rules on admissibility on the issue of guilt, and the Court of Appeals had effectively ruled the confession could not reduce Brady's offense below first-degree murder. Affirmed. Opinion of the Court by Justice Douglas, announced by Justice Brennan. The opinion text does not state the vote.

rule: In the field of public education, the doctrine of "separate but equal" has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal, so state laws requiring or permitting racial segregation in public schools deny Black children the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment, even when physical facilities and other "tangible" factors are equal.
holding: Yes. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal, so segregation in public education denies equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court (Chief Justice Warren delivering the opinion) announced this holding without entering final decrees and restored the cases to the docket for further argument on relief.

rule: Under Rule 56(c), after adequate time for discovery and upon motion, summary judgment must be entered against a party who fails to make a showing sufficient to establish an element essential to its case on which it will bear the burden of proof at trial. A moving party who will not bear that burden need not produce affidavits or other evidence negating the opponent's claim. It may discharge its initial burden by "showing," meaning pointing out to the district court, that there is an absence of evidence to support the nonmoving party's case. The nonmoving party must then go beyond the pleadings and designate specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial.
holding: No. Rule 56 contains no express or implied requirement that the movant submit evidence negating the opponent's claim, and the movant may meet its initial burden by pointing out the absence of evidence supporting the nonmovant's case; the judgment of the Court of Appeals is reversed and the case remanded (Rehnquist, J., for a 5-4 Court).

rule: When a court reviews an agency's construction of a statute the agency administers, it first asks whether Congress has directly spoken to the precise question at issue; if congressional intent is clear, the court and the agency must give it effect. If the statute is silent or ambiguous on the specific issue, the court may not impose its own construction and asks only whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible construction of the statute. A reasonable agency interpretation that reconciles competing policies within a gap left by Congress is entitled to deference, even if the agency has changed its view and even if it is not the reading the court would have chosen.
holding: Yes. Because Congress did not address whether the bubble concept applies to the nonattainment permit program, and EPA's plantwide definition is a permissible construction that seeks to accommodate progress in reducing air pollution with economic growth, the court must defer; the judgment of the Court of Appeals is reversed (opinion by Justice Stevens; the opinion does not state a vote count, and notes that Justices Marshall and Rehnquist took no part in the consideration or decision and Justice O'Connor took no part in the decision).

rule: Malice for murder does not require an intent to kill. When a person intentionally does an uncalled-for act in callous disregard of its likely harmful effects on others, under circumstances where he must reasonably anticipate that death is likely to result, that "wickedness of disposition" and "hardness of heart" is malice. A resulting death is second-degree murder. Second-degree murder in Pennsylvania includes every element of first-degree murder except the specific intent to kill.
holding: Yes. An intentional act of gross recklessness, done in wanton disregard of consequences the actor must reasonably anticipate are likely to cause death, shows malice and supports second-degree murder even without intent to kill, so all assignments of error are overruled and the judgment is affirmed (opinion by Chief Justice Maxey; the vote is not stated in the opinion text).

rule: Under the Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause, testimonial statements of a witness absent from trial are admissible against a criminal defendant only if the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. A judicial finding that a testimonial statement is reliable cannot substitute for confrontation, so the Ohio v. Roberts "indicia of reliability" test no longer governs testimonial hearsay. "Testimonial" covers, at a minimum, prior testimony at a preliminary hearing, before a grand jury, or at a former trial, and statements made in police interrogations.
holding: Yes. Testimonial statements of an absent witness are admissible only where the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine, Sylvia's police-interrogation statement was testimonial and untested by cross-examination, and so the judgment of the Washington Supreme Court is reversed and remanded (opinion by Justice Scalia; the opinion text does not state the vote).

rule: A defendant who raised no objection at trial to multiple representation must show that an actual conflict of interest adversely affected his lawyer's performance; the mere possibility of conflict is not enough. Once he shows that, he need not show prejudice. Absent an objection, a trial court has no Sixth Amendment duty to inquire into multiple representation unless it knows or reasonably should know that a particular conflict exists, and these rules apply equally to retained and appointed counsel.
holding: No; absent an objection at trial, a defendant must show that an actual conflict of interest adversely affected his lawyer's performance, so the Third Circuit's possible-conflict standard was wrong, and the judgment is vacated and remanded (opinion by Justice Powell; the text does not state the vote).

case_name: Escola v. Coca Cola Bottling Co.
rule: Res ipsa loquitur applies only if (1) defendant had exclusive control of the thing causing the injury and (2) the accident is of a kind that ordinarily would not occur without defendant's negligence. Where the accident happens after defendant gave up control, the control element is met if defendant controlled the instrumentality at the time of the alleged negligent act and plaintiff offers evidence permitting a reasonable inference that the instrumentality was not changed after leaving defendant's possession and was carefully handled by plaintiff and any third person. That showing satisfies only the control element. Plaintiff must still satisfy the second element, and the doctrine then supplies only an inference of negligence. Once the inference arises, whether defendant's rebuttal evidence dispels it is ordinarily a jury question.
holding: Yes. The evidence supported a reasonable inference that the bottle was not damaged after delivery, so it was defective when defendant relinquished control. Although it was unclear whether an excessive charge or a defect in the glass caused the explosion, there was a sufficient showing that neither cause would ordinarily have been present if due care had been used, and defendant had exclusive control over both charging and inspection. Plaintiff could therefore rely on res ipsa to supply an inference of negligence, and the jury could weigh defendant's rebuttal evidence; judgment affirmed (Gibson, C.J., joined by Shenk, Curtis, Carter, and Schauer, JJ.; Traynor, J., concurring in the judgment).

case_name: Florida Bar v. Went For It, Inc.
rule: Lawyer advertising is commercial speech. Commercial speech that is neither misleading nor about unlawful activity, like the advertising here, may be regulated if the government satisfies the three-prong Central Hudson test. A state bar may bar lawyers from sending targeted direct-mail solicitations to accident or disaster victims and their relatives for 30 days after the event. That ban serves a substantial interest in protecting victims' privacy and tranquility and the profession's reputation. The bar's unrebutted statistical and anecdotal record shows the ban advances that interest directly and materially. Its brief duration and the ample alternative channels left open make it a reasonable fit.
holding: No. The 30-day ban satisfies all three prongs of Central Hudson. The Bar has a substantial interest in victims' privacy and in public confidence in the profession, its unrebutted study shows the ban directly and materially advances that interest, and the ban is narrow in scope and duration. The Eleventh Circuit's judgment was reversed (Justice O'Connor for the Court; Justice Kennedy, joined by three Justices, dissenting).

rule: Battery requires an act done with the intent to bring about a harmful or offensive contact, and intent exists when the actor acts either for the purpose of causing the contact or with knowledge that the contact is substantially certain to result. Proof of substantial-certainty knowledge establishes intent even without any purpose to injure, embarrass, or play a prank. A child is subject to the same battery rules as an adult, and age matters only in deciding what the child actually knew.
holding: Yes. Battery intent is established if the actor knew with substantial certainty that the contact would result, even with no purpose to injure or embarrass. Because the trial court's findings did not expressly address Brian's knowledge, the case was remanded for clarification and for findings on that issue, with instructions to change the judgment if the findings warrant it. (Hill, J., with Schwellenbach, Donworth, and Weaver, JJ., concurring.)

rule: Congress's power to regulate commerce "among the several States" covers all commercial intercourse, including navigation and the carriage of passengers, that concerns more states than one. That power reaches into the interior of each state but stops short of commerce that is completely internal to a single state. Under the Supremacy Clause, a state law that collides with an act of Congress passed under this power must yield, even if the state enacted it in the exercise of powers acknowledged to remain with the states.
holding: Yes. Congress's commerce power includes navigation between states. The federal coasting license authorizes the licensed vessel to carry on that trade, so New York's laws collide with the act of Congress and must yield under the Supremacy Clause, and the New York decree sustaining the injunction was erroneous. (Opinion by Marshall, C.J.; no vote count appears in the opinion text.)

rule: Consideration exists when the promisee abandons a legal right or limits his lawful freedom of action as an inducement for the promise. A court will not ask whether that forbearance actually benefited the promisor, or whether it harmed or helped the promisee. Benefit to the promisor and detriment to the promisee are alternative branches, and legal detriment alone is enough.
holding: Yes. Giving up a legal right or restricting one's lawful freedom of action in exchange for a promise is sufficient consideration whether or not the promisor benefits, and the uncle's later letter, with the nephew's assent, created a trust that defeated the Statute of Limitations defense. The General Term's order was reversed and the Special Term judgment affirmed, with costs out of the estate (Parker, J., for a unanimous court: "All concur").

rule: Materials an attorney obtains or prepares in anticipation of litigation (witness statements, memoranda, mental impressions) fall outside the attorney-client privilege, yet they are not discoverable on mere demand. The party seeking them bears the burden of showing necessity or justification, such as that the facts are essential to its case and otherwise unavailable. An attorney's account of oral witness statements and mental impressions receives even stronger protection, and no showing of necessity sufficed to compel it on these facts.
holding: No. Such materials, though outside the attorney-client privilege, are not discoverable as of right, and the party seeking them must show adequate reasons justifying production, a showing petitioner never attempted. The Third Circuit's judgment is affirmed (opinion by Justice Murphy; the vote is not stated in the opinion text).

rule: Under Rule 1-103(a) of the Illinois Code of Professional Responsibility, a lawyer who possesses unprivileged knowledge that another lawyer has engaged in illegal conduct involving moral turpitude or conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation must report it to an authority empowered to investigate or act on it. The duty is the lawyer's own. A client's instruction not to report, the client's own complaint to the disciplinary authority, and the lawyer's lack of a dishonest motive are not defenses. Failure to report is sanctionable, and here warranted a one-year suspension.
holding: Yes. A lawyer with unprivileged knowledge of another lawyer's conversion of client funds must report it under Rule 1-103(a), and neither the client's wishes nor the client's own contact with the Commission excuses the failure; the court rejected the Review Board's recommendation and suspended respondent for one year (opinion by Justice Stamos; vote not stated in the text).

rule: Under the Uniform Parentage Act, a woman's motherhood may be established "under this part" (Fam. Code § 7610), and by parity of reasoning from the artificial insemination statute (Fam. Code § 7613), a married couple who consent to a medical procedure that results in a child's birth are the child's lawful parents even when neither has a biological tie to the child. Applying Johnson v. Calvert's reasoning to the circumstances here, where the intended mother and another woman could each establish motherhood under the Act, the tie is broken in favor of the intended mother. Parents cannot by agreement limit or abrogate a child's right to support.
holding: Yes. Because their consent to the medical procedure caused the child's conception and birth, Luanne and John are Jaycee's lawful parents under Fam. Code § 7610 and § 7613 applied by parity of reasoning, and John's paternity and support duty stand regardless of any promise by Luanne to assume sole responsibility. The court reversed the rulings that Luanne was not the lawful mother, that John was not the lawful father, and that no support was due. It remanded with directions to enter a new judgment declaring both lawful parents, to make all appropriate orders ensuring Luanne's legal custody, to amend the birth certificate to reflect Luanne as mother and John as lawful father, and to make an appropriate permanent child support order; until then, the temporary support order remains in effect. Opinion by Sills, P.J., with Wallin, J., and Crosby, J., concurring (unanimous panel).

rule: Under the Uniform Dissolution of Marriage Act's definition of "marital property" (§ 14-10-113(2), C.R.S. 1973), an educational degree such as an M.B.A. earned during the marriage is not property subject to division on dissolution. It lacks the usual attributes of property: exchange value, transferability, and inheritability. A spouse who financially supported the other's education may still have that contribution considered when the court divides whatever marital property exists, or as a relevant factor in awarding maintenance if maintenance is sought and need is shown.
holding: No. An M.B.A. degree is not "property" within the Act's definition of marital property because it has no exchange value, is personal to the holder, terminates at death, and cannot be transferred; the court of appeals' judgment is affirmed (opinion by Justice Lee, with Chief Justice Pringle and Justices Groves and Carrigan dissenting).

case_name: Javins v. First National Realty Corp.
rule: A warranty of habitability, measured by the standards of the D.C. Housing Regulations, is implied by operation of law into leases of urban dwelling units covered by those Regulations. The warranty cannot be waived, and breach gives the tenant the usual contract remedies. Because the tenant's duty to pay rent depends on the landlord's performance, the tenant may raise housing code violations as a defense in an eviction for nonpayment.
holding: Yes. A warranty of habitability measured by the Housing Regulations is implied into leases of covered urban dwellings, the tenant's rent obligation depends on the landlord's performance of that warranty, and the tenant must be allowed to prove violations. Reversed and remanded (opinion by Judge J. Skelly Wright; Judge Robb concurred only in the result and in Parts IV-B and V; the opinion does not state a vote count).

rule: Under California's Uniform Parentage Act, proof of genetic consanguinity (through blood testing) and proof of having given birth are both means of establishing a mother and child relationship, and California recognizes only one natural mother per child. When the two means do not coincide in one woman, the natural mother is the woman who intended to procreate the child, meaning she who intended to bring about the birth of a child she intended to raise as her own. A gestational surrogacy contract is not, on its face, inconsistent with public policy, and declaring the gestational surrogate not to be the legal mother does not violate the state or federal Constitution.
holding: Yes. When genetic consanguinity and giving birth are split between two women, the woman who intended to procreate and raise the child is the natural mother. That result does not offend the Constitution or public policy. The Court of Appeal's judgment was affirmed in an opinion by Panelli, J., joined by Lucas, C.J., and Mosk, Baxter, and George, JJ. Arabian, J., concurred separately, and Kennard, J., dissented.

rule: Under the discovery principle adopted by the United States, the discovering European sovereign, and the United States as its successor, holds the ultimate title to land in America, subject only to the Indian right of occupancy, and holds the exclusive right to extinguish that occupancy by purchase or conquest. Indian tribes may not convey the absolute title to private individuals, so a title resting solely on a direct purchase from a tribe cannot be sustained in U.S. courts.
holding: No. Discovery vested the ultimate title and the exclusive right to extinguish Indian occupancy in the discovering sovereign and its successor, so the tribes could not convey a title the courts will sustain, and the judgment was affirmed with costs (opinion by Chief Justice Marshall; vote not stated).

rule: A criminal defendant has no constitutional right to compel appointed appellate counsel to raise every nonfrivolous issue the defendant requests, if counsel, as a matter of professional judgment, decides not to present those points. The accused keeps ultimate authority over certain fundamental decisions: whether to plead guilty, waive a jury, testify in their own behalf, or take an appeal. Outside those decisions, strategic and tactical choices such as which issues to press on appeal belong to counsel, after consultation with the client.
holding: No; neither Anders nor any other decision gives an indigent defendant a constitutional right to compel appointed counsel to press nonfrivolous points that counsel, in professional judgment, decides not to present, so the Second Circuit's judgment is reversed (opinion by Chief Justice Burger).

rule: A property owner has no privilege to use force calculated to cause death or serious bodily injury to protect land or chattels unless the intruder also threatens the owner's personal safety enough to justify self-defense. An owner cannot do indirectly by a mechanical device, such as a spring gun, what the owner could not do in person. A spring gun or similar device is justified only against a trespasser committing a felony of violence or a felony punishable by death, or endangering human life. Breaking and entering an unoccupied house to steal does not qualify, and the trespasser's own illegal conduct does not change the rule.
holding: No. An owner may not use deadly or seriously injurious force, including by a spring gun, to protect property where no human life is threatened, so the trial court's instructions were correct and the judgment was affirmed (opinion by Moore, C.J.; all justices concurred except Larson, J., who dissented).

case_name: Kelo v. City of New London
rule: Under the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause, "public use" means "public purpose," and courts give broad deference to legislative judgments about what public needs justify a taking. A city's taking of private, non-blighted property to carry out a carefully considered, integrated economic development plan satisfies the public use requirement, even when the land will be transferred to private parties. The government may not take A's property for the sole purpose of transferring it to private party B. It also may not take property under a mere pretext of public purpose when its actual purpose is to confer a private benefit.
holding: Yes. Because the city's comprehensive development plan serves a public purpose, and the Court has long read "public use" broadly as "public purpose" with deference to legislative judgment, the takings satisfy the Fifth Amendment. The judgment of the Connecticut Supreme Court is affirmed (opinion by Stevens, J.).

rule: A statute that classifies by race does not escape the Equal Protection Clause because it punishes members of each race equally. Racial classifications, especially in criminal statutes, receive the "most rigid scrutiny" and must be shown necessary to accomplish a permissible state objective independent of racial discrimination. The freedom to marry is a vital personal right and one of the "basic civil rights of man," and restricting it on the basis of racial classifications also violates the Due Process Clause.
holding: Yes. Virginia's antimiscegenation statutes rest solely on racial classifications that serve no legitimate overriding purpose independent of invidious racial discrimination, and they deprive the Lovings of the fundamental freedom to marry without due process, so the convictions are reversed (opinion by Chief Justice Warren; the opinion text does not state the vote).

rule: Due process does not require a State to let a biological father rebut the marital presumption and obtain parental rights to a child conceived and born into an existing marriage, where the mother and her husband were cohabiting and both wish to raise the child as their own. Under the plurality's approach, a claimed liberty interest must be fundamental and rooted in history and tradition, and no tradition protects the adulterous natural father's claim against the marital family. The plurality reviewed a child's equal protection challenge to her exclusion from rebutting the presumption under rational basis.
holding: No. Affirmed. Justice Scalia announced the judgment in a plurality opinion. A four-Justice plurality (Scalia, Rehnquist, O'Connor, and Kennedy) concluded that the presumption denies no constitutionally protected liberty interest of the father, that the child's due process claim fails even assuming she has a liberty interest, and that her equal protection claim fails rational basis review. Justice Stevens concurred only in the judgment: he assumed Michael had a protected interest but found that Michael received a fair opportunity to seek visitation under § 4601. The judgment drew five votes as reflected in the joins (Scalia, Rehnquist, O'Connor, Kennedy, and Stevens concurring in the judgment), over dissents by Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun, and White.

case_name: Moore v. City of East Cleveland
rule: When the government intrudes on choices concerning family living arrangements, the usual judicial deference to land-use legislation does not apply, and the court must examine carefully the importance of the governmental interests advanced and the extent to which the regulation serves them (plurality). The family protected by the Due Process Clause is defined by the Nation's history and tradition, and that tradition extends beyond the nuclear family to relatives such as grandparents, uncles, aunts, and cousins sharing a household. A housing ordinance that criminalizes a grandmother living with her grandson because of which relatives are in the home fails that scrutiny.
holding: Yes, according to the plurality; the judgment was reversed. Justice Powell announced the judgment of the Court and wrote an opinion for four Justices (himself and Justices Brennan, Marshall, and Blackmun). That plurality concluded that the ordinance's intrusion into family living arrangements requires careful examination of the city's interests, and that the ordinance serves its legitimate goals only marginally and therefore violates due process. This due-process rationale did not command a majority. Justice Stevens supplied the fifth vote for reversal, concurring only in the judgment on the separate ground that the ordinance was an impermissible restriction on Mrs. Moore's right to use her property.

rule: Under New York's Equitable Distribution Law, a professional license acquired during the marriage is "marital property" under Domestic Relations Law § 236 (B) (1) (c) and is subject to equitable distribution. The license's value is the enhanced earning capacity it gives the holder. The non-licensed spouse is entitled to an equitable portion of that value, usually through a distributive award under § 236 (B) (5) (e), and is not limited to reimbursement of direct financial contributions.
holding: Yes. A medical license acquired during marriage is marital property under § 236 (B) (1) (c) and subject to equitable distribution under § 236 (B) (5), so the Appellate Division's order was modified by reinstating the trial court's judgment, the case was remitted to the Appellate Division for determination of the facts and exercise of its discretion, and, as modified, affirmed (Simons, J., for a unanimous court; Wachtler, C.J., and Jasen, Meyer, Kaye, Alexander, and Titone, JJ., concurring).

case_name: Ohralik v. Ohio State Bar Ass'n
rule: A State, or a Bar acting with state authorization, may constitutionally discipline a lawyer for soliciting clients in person, for pecuniary gain, under circumstances likely to pose dangers the State has a right to prevent. Because the anti-solicitation rules are prophylactic, the State need not prove actual harm to the person solicited. In-person commercial solicitation gets some First Amendment protection, but a lower level of scrutiny than truthful advertising under Bates.
holding: No. A State may discipline a lawyer for in-person solicitation for pecuniary gain under circumstances likely to produce the harms it seeks to prevent, and proof of actual injury is immaterial, so applying DR 2-103(A) and 2-104(A) to Ohralik did not offend the Constitution. Affirmed (opinion by Justice Powell; Justice Brennan took no part).

rule: A gender classification survives equal protection scrutiny only if it serves important governmental objectives and is substantially related to achieving them, and this applies equally when the classification burdens men. A statute that lets courts order alimony from husbands but never from wives fails that test, because the State already holds individualized hearings on the parties' finances and so has no need to use sex as a proxy for need or for past discrimination. Even statutes meant to compensate women for past discrimination must be carefully tailored, and the State may not classify by sex when a gender-neutral rule would serve its purposes as well.
holding: Yes. In an opinion by Justice Brennan, the Court held the Alabama alimony statutes unconstitutional because the gender classification is not substantially related to the State's important objectives where individualized hearings already assess each spouse's need, and it reversed and remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with the opinion.

rule: A state court may not rely on private racial prejudice, or the injury that prejudice might cause a child, as a ground for removing a child from the custody of a parent found to be an appropriate custodian. A custody decision that rests on race is a racial classification by the state and gets the most exacting scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause. The best-interests goal is a substantial governmental interest, but the effects of racial prejudice, however real, cannot justify a racial classification that removes the child.
holding: No. Private racial biases and the possible injury they might inflict are impermissible considerations for removing a child from the custody of a natural mother found to be an appropriate custodian, so the judgment of the District Court of Appeal is reversed (opinion by Chief Justice Burger; the vote is not stated in the opinion text).

rule: Prenuptial agreements are contracts and are judged by the same standards as other contracts. Absent fraud, misrepresentation, or duress, spouses are bound by their terms, and courts will not review whether the bargain was reasonable at signing or at divorce, whether a party understood the rights surrendered, or whether a party had independent counsel. The parties must still make a full and fair (though not exact) disclosure of their financial positions. A recital of full disclosure in the agreement creates a presumption of full disclosure, which a spouse alleging fraud or misrepresentation can rebut only by clear and convincing evidence.
holding: Yes. A prenuptial agreement is enforceable under ordinary contract principles when there is full and fair financial disclosure and no fraud, misrepresentation, or duress, without inquiry into reasonableness, understanding of rights, or access to counsel. Order affirmed (Flaherty, J., for the Court; Papadakos, J., concurring in the result only; McDermott, J., joined by Larsen, J., dissenting).

rule: A court may, in its discretion under Rule 60.02(6), vacate a settlement it approved on behalf of a minor when the minor had a serious injury that was not known or considered when the court approved the settlement. Relief is available without fraud, bad faith, or a mutual mistake when one party knew of the injury and knew that neither the court nor the minor's side knew of it. This holds even if no canon of ethics or legal obligation required that party's counsel to disclose the information.
holding: Yes. A court may vacate a minor's settlement for a unilateral mistake where the opposing party knew of an injury that neither the court nor the minor's side knew of, so the settlement did not account for it, and the trial court did not abuse its discretion. Affirmed (opinion by Justice Thomas Gallagher; the opinion does not state the vote; Justice Rogosheske took no part).

rule: Under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, a parent, including an unwed father who has sired and raised his children, is entitled to a hearing on his fitness before the State removes his children from his custody. A State may not substitute a conclusive presumption of unfitness based on marital status for an individualized determination merely because presuming is cheaper and easier than proving. Granting fitness hearings to married parents and unwed mothers while denying them to unwed fathers violates the Equal Protection Clause.
holding: Yes; as a matter of due process, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken, and denying him that hearing while extending it to all other parents denied him equal protection, so the judgment of the Illinois Supreme Court is reversed and the case remanded (opinion by Justice White; Justice Douglas joined Parts I and II only; Justices Powell and Rehnquist did not participate).

rule: A defendant claiming actual ineffective assistance of counsel under the Sixth Amendment must show (1) deficient performance, meaning counsel's representation fell below an objective standard of reasonableness under prevailing professional norms, judged with strong deference and from counsel's perspective at the time, and (2) prejudice, meaning a reasonable probability that, but for counsel's unprofessional errors, the result of the proceeding would have been different. A reasonable probability is a probability sufficient to undermine confidence in the outcome. Prejudice is assessed under the governing legal standard, assuming a decisionmaker who acts lawfully and is reasonably, conscientiously, and impartially applying that standard. For a death sentence, the question is whether there is a reasonable probability the sentencer would have concluded that the balance of aggravating and mitigating circumstances did not warrant death. Failure on either prong defeats the claim.
holding: No; under the two-part test of deficient performance and resulting prejudice, counsel's conduct was reasonable professional judgment, and even if it were not, there was no reasonable probability the omitted evidence would have changed the sentence, so the judgment of the Court of Appeals was reversed (opinion by Justice O'Connor).

case_name: Togstad v. Vesely, Otto, Miller & Keefe
rule: A legal malpractice plaintiff must show (1) an attorney-client relationship, (2) negligence or breach of contract by the attorney, (3) proximate cause of damages, and (4) that but for the attorney's conduct the plaintiff would have succeeded on the underlying claim. An attorney-client relationship can arise, under either a tort or a contract theory, when a person seeks and receives legal advice from a lawyer under circumstances that make it reasonably foreseeable to the lawyer that the person will be injured if the advice is negligently given. A lawyer who gives an opinion on the merits of a medical malpractice claim without the minimal research an ordinarily prudent attorney would do, or without mentioning a soon-to-expire limitations period, may be found negligent.
holding: Yes; under either a tort or a contract analysis, a jury could find an attorney-client relationship where Mrs. Togstad sought and received legal advice from Miller under circumstances making it reasonably foreseeable that she would be injured by negligent advice, and the record supported the findings of negligence, causation, and damages, so the judgment was affirmed (per curiam; no vote is stated).

rule: The Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children. Fit parents are presumed to act in their children's best interests, so when a fit parent's visitation decision is subject to judicial review, the court must accord at least some special weight to the parent's own determination. A nonparental visitation statute of sweeping breadth is unconstitutional as applied where the trial court gives a fit parent's decision no special weight and the order rests on nothing more than a simple disagreement with the parent about the child's best interests. The plurality did not define the precise scope of the parental right in the visitation context.
holding: Yes. Resting on the "sweeping breadth" of §26.10.160(3) together with the trial court's application of it, the plurality held the statute unconstitutional as applied to Granville and her family. The application featured a combination of factors: no allegation or finding that Granville was unfit; no special weight given to her determination, with the court instead applying a presumption in favor of grandparent visitation; no weight given to her having already offered meaningful visitation; and only slender findings. Taken together, these showed that the order reflected nothing more than a simple disagreement between the court and Granville about her children's best interests, and the order violated her substantive due process right. The judgment of the Washington Supreme Court is affirmed (plurality opinion by Justice O'Connor, joined by the Chief Justice, Justice Ginsburg, and Justice Breyer; Justices Souter and Thomas concurred in the judgment; Justices Stevens, Scalia, and Kennedy dissented).

rule: When a prison regulation impinges on inmates' constitutional rights, the regulation is valid if it is reasonably related to legitimate penological interests. Inmates keep the fundamental right to marry recognized in Zablocki and Loving. A rule barring inmate marriage unless the superintendent finds "compelling reasons" is an exaggerated response to security and rehabilitation concerns and fails even this deferential standard.
holding: Yes: prison regulations burdening inmates' constitutional rights are tested by whether they are reasonably related to legitimate penological interests, and the near-total marriage ban fails that test and is facially invalid, so the judgment striking the marriage rule is affirmed, the judgment striking the correspondence rule is reversed, and the case is remanded on whether the correspondence rule was applied arbitrarily (opinion by Justice O'Connor; the opinion text does not state the vote).

rule: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 501, the corporate attorney-client privilege is not limited to the "control group" of senior managers. Declining to lay down a general rule, the Court held that the control group test cannot govern the development of the law in this area. On the facts before it, the Court held that Upjohn employees' communications to corporate counsel were privileged. Those communications were made at the direction of corporate superiors to secure legal advice, concerned matters within the employees' duties, were made by employees aware of the legal purpose, and were kept confidential. The work-product doctrine applies to IRS summonses, and attorney notes and memoranda of witnesses' oral statements cannot be compelled on a mere showing of substantial need and undue hardship.
holding: Yes; in an opinion by Justice Rehnquist, the Court held that the employees' communications to counsel were privileged because the control group test frustrates the privilege's purpose, and that the work-product doctrine applies to IRS summonses with heightened protection for attorney notes of oral witness statements, so the judgment was reversed and remanded.

rule: The Sixth Amendment creates a presumption in favor of a criminal defendant's counsel of choice. A trial court may overcome that presumption, and refuse a defendant's waiver of conflict-free counsel, on a showing of an actual conflict or of a serious potential for conflict. Trial courts get substantial latitude in making this call, and the evaluation of each case is left primarily to the trial court's informed judgment.
holding: No; the presumption in favor of counsel of choice can be overcome by an actual conflict or a serious potential for conflict, the District Court's refusal here was within its discretion, and the judgment of the Court of Appeals is affirmed (opinion by Chief Justice Rehnquist).

rule: When parents' traditional interest in directing the religious upbringing of their children is combined with a free exercise claim, the State must show more than a "reasonable relation to some purpose within the competency of the State" to enforce a generally applicable law against them. Only state interests "of the highest order and those not otherwise served" can overbalance a legitimate free exercise claim. Parental power remains subject to limitation under Prince v. Massachusetts if parental decisions will jeopardize the child's health or safety or have a potential for significant social burdens.
holding: Yes. Because the compulsory-attendance law severely burdened the Amish parents' free exercise of religion and the State failed to show with particularity how its interest in education would be harmed by exempting the Amish after the eighth grade, the State cannot compel respondents to cause their children to attend formal high school to age 16; affirmed (opinion by Chief Justice Burger; Justices Powell and Rehnquist took no part).

rule: The right to marry is of fundamental importance. A statutory classification that significantly interferes with the decision to marry cannot be upheld unless it is supported by sufficiently important state interests and is closely tailored to effectuate only those interests. Reasonable regulations that do not significantly interfere with decisions to enter into marriage may still be imposed without rigorous scrutiny.
holding: Yes. Because § 245.10 directly and substantially interferes with the fundamental right to marry, and the means chosen unnecessarily impinge on that right given the State's asserted interests, the classification fails critical examination under the Equal Protection Clause; the judgment of the District Court is affirmed (opinion by Justice Marshall).
